ככה אני מבין איך מחזיקים תינוק,
ושצריך להיות עדינים.

תגידו לי את האמת
שהתינוק יהיה מתוק, אבל גם יבכה.
הרבה. גם בלילה.
ושאמא תהיה איתו הרבה זמן.
אם אני יודע את זה מראש,
אני לא מופתע כשזה קורה.

מי לוקח אותי לגן,
מי מקריא לי סיפור בלילה,

אולי אני אהיה שמח. אולי אכעס.
אולי גם וגם.
ואם אני לא רוצה לדבר על התינוק,
אל תכריחו אותי.

שאתם אוהבים אותי בדיוק אותו דבר.

sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 10 Feb 2026)
sources.quote: Find chances to talk about baby. ... Remind your child about when they were a baby. Show your child their baby pictures. ... Consider giving your child a doll so that they can take care of "their" baby. This helps explain what being around a baby is like. ... Be honest. Explain that the baby will be cute but will also cry and take a lot of your time and attention. ... when they play or help care for baby, that they need to be gentle. Reassure your child that you will love them just as much after the baby is born, as you do now. ... Involve your preschooler in planning for baby. This will make them less jealous. Let them shop with you for baby items. ... Time major changes in your child's routine. If you can, finish toilet training or switching from a crib to a bed before the baby arrives. ... Prepare your child for when you are in the hospital. ... Explain that you will be back with the new baby in a few days. ... Expect your child to regress a little. ... Set aside special time for your child. ... make them feel that they are a part of things by having them cuddle next to you when you feed the baby. ... Find ways to invite your child to help. ... Ask family and friends to spend time with your older child when they come to see the new baby. This will help them feel special and not left out. ... Continue to read children's books about newborns and siblings with your child. ... Explain to your child that sometimes you need to take care of baby first.
sources.supports: A page from the American Academy of Pediatrics with steps to prepare an older child for a new baby: talk about the baby, baby pictures, a doll, honesty about crying and gentleness, a promise of love, involving the child in planning and shopping, timing major changes, a plan for the hospital days, special one on one time, a role in helping, cuddling next to the parent during feeding, relatives who spend time with the older child, books about newborns and siblings, and explaining that sometimes the baby is cared for first. It lists toddlers and preschoolers by age; we apply it to ages 4 and 5.

sources.title: Preparing Your Child for a New Sibling
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts)
sources.quote: Preschoolers, for example, may not grasp concepts of time, so it might not mean much if you say that the baby will arrive in a few months. It may be more useful to explain that the baby will arrive in a particular season, such as winter or when it's cold outside. ... going through your child's baby pictures ... reading books about childbirth (make sure they're age-appropriate) ... packing a bag for the hospital ... going to the doctor to hear the baby's heartbeat ... As your due date draws near, make arrangements for older kids for the time when you're in the hospital. Discuss these plans so kids know what to expect when the day arrives. ... Consider letting your child visit you in the hospital as soon as possible after the baby is born ... Try to keep routines as regular as possible in the days and weeks around the baby's arrival. ... Take advantage of chances for one-on-one time with older kids. Spend time together while the baby is sleeping ... Also remind relatives and friends that your older child might want to talk about something other than the new baby. ... Continue to send your older child to childcare or to school, if you're able. ... If your child expresses no interest in the baby, don't be alarmed and don't force it. It can take time. ... Encourage older kids to talk about their feelings about the new baby.
sources.supports: A Nemours KidsHealth page for parents: explain the arrival with a season for preschoolers, baby pictures, books, a hospital bag, hearing the heartbeat, a plan for the hospital days that the child knows in advance, an early hospital visit, regular routines, one on one time, relatives who ask about the older child too, gan or school as usual, no forcing when the child shows no interest, and talking about feelings.

sources.quote: Find chances to talk about baby. ... Remind your child about when they were a baby. Show your child their baby pictures. ... Consider giving your child a doll so that they can take care of "their" baby. This helps explain what being around a baby is like. ... Be honest. Explain that the baby will be cute but will also cry and take a lot of your time and attention. ... when they play or help care for baby, that they need to be gentle. Reassure your child that you will love them just as much after the baby is born, as you do now. ... Involve your preschooler in planning for baby. This will make them less jealous. Let them shop with you for baby items. ... Time major changes in your child's routine. If you can, finish toilet training or switching from a crib to a bed before the baby arrives. ... Prepare your child for when you are in the hospital. ... Explain that you will be back with the new baby in a few days. ... Expect your child to regress a little. ... Set aside special time for your child. ... make them feel that they are a part of things by having them cuddle next to you when you feed the baby. ... Find ways to invite your child to help. ... Ask family and friends to spend time with your older child when they come to see the new baby. This will help them feel special and not left out. ... Continue to read children's books about newborns and siblings with your child. ... Explain to your child that sometimes you need to take care of baby first.

sources.quote: Preschoolers, for example, may not grasp concepts of time, so it might not mean much if you say that the baby will arrive in a few months. It may be more useful to explain that the baby will arrive in a particular season, such as winter or when it's cold outside. ... going through your child's baby pictures ... reading books about childbirth (make sure they're age-appropriate) ... packing a bag for the hospital ... going to the doctor to hear the baby's heartbeat ... As your due date draws near, make arrangements for older kids for the time when you're in the hospital. Discuss these plans so kids know what to expect when the day arrives. ... Consider letting your child visit you in the hospital as soon as possible after the baby is born ... Try to keep routines as regular as possible in the days and weeks around the baby's arrival. ... Take advantage of chances for one-on-one time with older kids. Spend time together while the baby is sleeping ... Also remind relatives and friends that your older child might want to talk about something other than the new baby. ... Continue to send your older child to childcare or to school, if you're able. ... If your child expresses no interest in the baby, don't be alarmed and don't force it. It can take time. ... Encourage older kids to talk about their feelings about the new baby.

sources.title: How to Share Books With Your Baby
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics Council on Early Childhood (last updated 29 Sep 2024)
sources.quote: Set aside a few quiet minutes for sharing books as part of your baby's regular naptime or bedtime routine. ... Shared reading should be fun, not forced. ... Remember that you never need to read the whole story. ... Babies love repetition. Don't be surprised if they like sharing the same book or certain parts of one again and again. ... Pay attention to a book for a few minutes at a time.
sources.supports: An AAP page on sharing books with a baby in the first year: books as part of the naptime or bedtime routine, shared reading should be fun and not forced, a parent never needs to read the whole story, babies love repetition, and babies pay attention to a book for a few minutes at a time. We apply it to a child of about 18 months as a continuation, and say so.

sources.title: Toddler Reading Time
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Kandia N. Lewis, PhD, reviewed August 2023)
sources.quote: Choosing regular times to read (especially before naps and bedtime) helps kids learn to sit with a book and relax. ... If your toddler will let you, hold them in your lap when you read. This helps your toddler feel safe, happy, and relaxed. ... Toddlers like to do things on their own. Encourage this by putting out three or four books and asking your child to pick one. ... Let your toddler help you turn pages ... When you come to a familiar or repetitive phrase or rhyme in a book, pause and let your child finish. ... Read whatever books your toddler asks for, even if it's the same book every night for weeks and weeks (and weeks and weeks). ... Read slowly so your toddler can understand the story. ... Read expressively, using different voices for different characters ... Use puppets, finger plays (like the "Itsy Bitsy Spider"), or props while you read. ... Encourage your toddler to clap or sing when you read rhythmic, sing-song books. ... Talk about the pictures. Point to items and name them. ... Use your child's name as the name of a character in the book. ... Trying to read to a toddler who won't sit still can be frustrating. ... If that doesn't work, don't force the reading but be sure to try again later. ... Some busy toddlers like to stand up while you read to them. ... toddlers' attention spans will get longer soon ... You might want to keep reading even if your child moves around. ... Before bedtime, allow your child to touch and play with favorite toys while you read aloud. ... Some kids might not look at you or the book, but that doesn't mean they're not interested or listening. ... If you feel tense or your toddler resists, consider setting the book aside and returning to it later. ... Keep your toddler's interest by choosing books with small amounts of words on the page ... Books about bedtime, baths, or mealtime are all good choices ... Keep books in a basket on the floor or on a low shelf where your child can reach them and look at them by themselves. ... Keep some books in the car and always have a few handy in your bag for long waits at the doctor or lines at the grocery store. ... Reading together regularly can strengthen that connection, helping your toddler feel safe and comfortable.
sources.supports: A KidsHealth page on reading with toddlers (the section Sitting Still Is Not Required): a toddler who won't sit still is common, standing or moving is fine, reading can continue, toys in hand are fine, not looking does not mean not listening, no forcing and a return later, three or four books to choose from, regular times before naps and bedtime, a lap if the child allows, books within reach in a basket, books in the bag, repetition, turning pages, pausing so the child finishes a phrase, voices, puppets and finger plays, clapping and singing, naming pictures, few words per page, everyday topics and the child's name as a character. Ages 12 to 36 months.

sources.title: How to Share Books With Your Baby
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics Council on Early Childhood (last updated 29 Sep 2024)
sources.quote: Set aside a few quiet minutes for sharing books as part of your baby's regular naptime or bedtime routine. ... Shared reading should be fun, not forced. ... Remember that you never need to read the whole story. ... Babies love repetition. Don't be surprised if they like sharing the same book or certain parts of one again and again. ... Pay attention to a book for a few minutes at a time.
sources.supports: An AAP page on sharing books with a baby in the first year: books as part of the naptime or bedtime routine, shared reading should be fun and not forced, a parent never needs to read the whole story, babies love repetition, and babies pay attention to a book for a few minutes at a time. We apply it to a child of about 18 months as a continuation, and say so.

sources.title: Toddler Reading Time
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Kandia N. Lewis, PhD, reviewed August 2023)
sources.quote: Choosing regular times to read (especially before naps and bedtime) helps kids learn to sit with a book and relax. ... If your toddler will let you, hold them in your lap when you read. This helps your toddler feel safe, happy, and relaxed. ... Toddlers like to do things on their own. Encourage this by putting out three or four books and asking your child to pick one. ... Let your toddler help you turn pages ... When you come to a familiar or repetitive phrase or rhyme in a book, pause and let your child finish. ... Read whatever books your toddler asks for, even if it's the same book every night for weeks and weeks (and weeks and weeks). ... Read slowly so your toddler can understand the story. ... Read expressively, using different voices for different characters ... Use puppets, finger plays (like the "Itsy Bitsy Spider"), or props while you read. ... Encourage your toddler to clap or sing when you read rhythmic, sing-song books. ... Talk about the pictures. Point to items and name them. ... Use your child's name as the name of a character in the book. ... Trying to read to a toddler who won't sit still can be frustrating. ... If that doesn't work, don't force the reading but be sure to try again later. ... Some busy toddlers like to stand up while you read to them. ... toddlers' attention spans will get longer soon ... You might want to keep reading even if your child moves around. ... Before bedtime, allow your child to touch and play with favorite toys while you read aloud. ... Some kids might not look at you or the book, but that doesn't mean they're not interested or listening. ... If you feel tense or your toddler resists, consider setting the book aside and returning to it later. ... Keep your toddler's interest by choosing books with small amounts of words on the page ... Books about bedtime, baths, or mealtime are all good choices ... Keep books in a basket on the floor or on a low shelf where your child can reach them and look at them by themselves. ... Keep some books in the car and always have a few handy in your bag for long waits at the doctor or lines at the grocery store. ... Reading together regularly can strengthen that connection, helping your toddler feel safe and comfortable.
sources.supports: A KidsHealth page on reading with toddlers (the section Sitting Still Is Not Required): a toddler who won't sit still is common, standing or moving is fine, reading can continue, toys in hand are fine, not looking does not mean not listening, no forcing and a return later, three or four books to choose from, regular times before naps and bedtime, a lap if the child allows, books within reach in a basket, books in the bag, repetition, turning pages, pausing so the child finishes a phrase, voices, puppets and finger plays, clapping and singing, naming pictures, few words per page, everyday topics and the child's name as a character. Ages 12 to 36 months.

sources.title: Toddler Reading Time
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Kandia N. Lewis, PhD, reviewed August 2023)
sources.quote: Choosing regular times to read (especially before naps and bedtime) helps kids learn to sit with a book and relax. ... If your toddler will let you, hold them in your lap when you read. This helps your toddler feel safe, happy, and relaxed. ... Toddlers like to do things on their own. Encourage this by putting out three or four books and asking your child to pick one. ... Let your toddler help you turn pages ... When you come to a familiar or repetitive phrase or rhyme in a book, pause and let your child finish. ... Read whatever books your toddler asks for, even if it's the same book every night for weeks and weeks (and weeks and weeks). ... Read slowly so your toddler can understand the story. ... Read expressively, using different voices for different characters ... Use puppets, finger plays (like the "Itsy Bitsy Spider"), or props while you read. ... Encourage your toddler to clap or sing when you read rhythmic, sing-song books. ... Talk about the pictures. Point to items and name them. ... Use your child's name as the name of a character in the book. ... Trying to read to a toddler who won't sit still can be frustrating. ... If that doesn't work, don't force the reading but be sure to try again later. ... Some busy toddlers like to stand up while you read to them. ... toddlers' attention spans will get longer soon ... You might want to keep reading even if your child moves around. ... Before bedtime, allow your child to touch and play with favorite toys while you read aloud. ... Some kids might not look at you or the book, but that doesn't mean they're not interested or listening. ... If you feel tense or your toddler resists, consider setting the book aside and returning to it later. ... Keep your toddler's interest by choosing books with small amounts of words on the page ... Books about bedtime, baths, or mealtime are all good choices ... Keep books in a basket on the floor or on a low shelf where your child can reach them and look at them by themselves. ... Keep some books in the car and always have a few handy in your bag for long waits at the doctor or lines at the grocery store. ... Reading together regularly can strengthen that connection, helping your toddler feel safe and comfortable.
sources.supports: A KidsHealth page on reading with toddlers (the section Sitting Still Is Not Required): a toddler who won't sit still is common, standing or moving is fine, reading can continue, toys in hand are fine, not looking does not mean not listening, no forcing and a return later, three or four books to choose from, regular times before naps and bedtime, a lap if the child allows, books within reach in a basket, books in the bag, repetition, turning pages, pausing so the child finishes a phrase, voices, puppets and finger plays, clapping and singing, naming pictures, few words per page, everyday topics and the child's name as a character. Ages 12 to 36 months.
